newsitem.title: UK: Europe Crude Outlook - Mean margins start to bite.
newsitem.headline: Europe Crude Outlook - Mean margins start to bite.

text.p: Emaciated refinery margins and rising Atlantic Basin supply should combine to give a broadly balanced North Sea crude market a softer tone this week, industry sources said.

With simple refineries in Northwest Europe running at loss-making levels and more complex plants struggling to return more than $1 a barrel cracking Brent, senior traders expected most North Sea grades to ease.

The exception could be benchmark Dated Brent, which appeared to be supported by demand from one trading house, Glencore, which paid July Brent +17 cents on Friday, 19 cents above the previous reported deal.
Some traders said Glencore was collecting Brents for shipment out of the region but others suggested the deal had more to do with influencing benchmark quotes.
"I think there's a pricing reason behind that deal and they'll probably sell Brent back into Europe. They're very short (Brent) CFDs next week," said a trader.
Brent Contracts for Difference (CFDs) for May 27-30 leapt on Friday to July Brent +14/+10 cents but the June 2-6 period was lagging badly at July Brent -15/-10 cents, dealers said.
Whatever the motivation, the sharp rally in Dated Brent has increased the pressure on European refineries to scale back crude throughputs as product prices fail to keep pace.

BP and Texaco have trimmed crude runs at their 400,000 barrels per day (bpd) joint venture refinery in Rotterdam by 10 percent for the month of May. Others were monitoring the situation closely, traders said.
"It would surprise me if you could sustain Brent at that level because it's really eating into the margin," said one.
Some North Sea sellers expected grade differentials to rise as a result of Dated's rally and thin early June supply.
But most traders were sceptical, pointing to sluggish demand across Europe -- Mediterranean refiners are also struggling with poor yields -- and fewer export opportunities to the U.S. Gulf.

"I think the U.S. has taken all the Brent it needs for now and while a lot of West African has gone east in the first half of June, it looks like it will be different story in the second (half)," said a trader.

A slide in Dubai margins in Singapore, where prompt gas oil traded below $25 a tonne for the first time since August last year, and a wider Brent-Dubai spread were making Nigerian sales to the Far East much more difficult.

"Eastbound chartering from West African terminals is on the way down and westbound chartering from the Middle East is rising sharply," said industry consultants Oil Movements in a report released last week.
A big jump in June crude contract formula prices set by the Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC) this week was also likely to reduce the scope for holders of June barrels.
Russian sour Urals crude could edge higher with much of the prompt May overhang mopped up in active trade last week, but poor refining margins would ensure any gains are modest, traders said.
